title: Government and Regulation
summary: How federal, state and local government split the work and the money, which regulators matter for which industries, and how tariffs work. Regulation is often the hidden constraint in a US case, and public-sector cases follow different rules.

blocks.title: Three layers, real power at each
blocks.body: The US is a federation: states are not administrative arms of Washington. They set their own taxes, minimum wages, licensing, insurance rules and much of healthcare and education policy. Counties and cities run schools (via school districts), police, zoning and local roads. A national rollout can therefore hit 50 different rulebooks. Always ask which level of government controls the lever in your case.

blocks.title: Who funds what
rows: ~87% state/local, ~13% federal (FY2023, NCES); property taxes matter locally
Federal share ~65% overall (FY2024); 50-77% by state, 90% for ACA expansion adults
Federal grants, states build and maintain

blocks.title: Antitrust basics for M&A cases
items: Large deals must be notified to the FTC and DOJ before closing (Hart-Scott-Rodino review).
Regulators look at market concentration and effects on prices, quality and innovation.
Remedies include blocking the deal, suing, or requiring divestitures of overlapping businesses.
Enforcement intensity shifts with each administration; build approval risk and timing into synergy cases.

blocks.title: Tariffs and trade basics
items: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the US importer of record and collected by Customs and Border Protection.
Who bears it economically depends on pass-through: importer margin, supplier price cuts, or consumer prices.
Section 232: national-security tariffs (e.g. steel, aluminum, autos). Section 301: response to unfair trade practices.
In February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled IEEPA emergency powers do not authorize tariffs; other authorities were then used.
The US ran a goods and services trade deficit of ~$900B in 2025, with a services surplus (BEA).

blocks.title: Model tariffs as a scenario
blocks.body: US trade policy changed repeatedly in 2025-26. In a sourcing or pricing case, avoid assuming one rate. Show a base and high-tariff scenario, ask what share of COGS is imported and from where, and discuss levers: re-sourcing, pass-through pricing, supplier cost sharing, and USMCA-qualifying supply.

blocks.title: State rules are not footnotes
blocks.body: Insurance, alcohol sales, car dealerships, professional licensing, data privacy and many healthcare rules vary by state. A strategy that works in Texas may be illegal or uneconomic in California. Ask which states the client operates in before assuming a national answer.

in_a_case: M&A case between two large competitors: raise FTC/DOJ review early, estimate timeline risk, and identify assets that might need divesting.
State Medicaid agency cost case: remember the federal match; a state dollar saved can mean losing more than a dollar of federal funds.
Manufacturer facing tariffs: split COGS by country of origin, then test pass-through, re-sourcing and supplier negotiations under scenarios.
School district or city client: budget is fixed by fiscal year and appropriation; prioritize low-capex, quick-win operational fixes and stakeholder buy-in.
Drug or device launch: FDA approval timing drives the revenue curve; CMS coverage rules then drive uptake.
